item.title: Ukraine war briefing: Trump accuses Zelenskyy of not wanting to end war as feud rumbles on
item.description:
Trump defends decision to waive some sanctions on Russia; Lithuania foils attack on Starlink site; Kyiv hits another oil terminal. What we know on day 1,699

Donald Trump has defended his decision to waive some sanctions on Russia, while once again accusing Volodymyr Zelenskyy of not wanting to end the war. “My decision on Russia is a very simple one. I am in the process of negotiating Peace in the war between Russia and Ukraine, and don’t want to do anything that will drive, foolishly, Russia away from the bargaining table,” the US president wrote on Truth Social. “Zelenskyy doesn’t care, and frankly, with all of the money that Europe is famously giving him … he doesn’t want to end this war, and probably never did,” he added. Trump’s remarks come after he signed an executive order on Friday putting on hold a sweeping new sanctions package targeting the Russian economy.

Earlier on Sunday, Zelenskyy had thanked the Trump administration for resuming intelligence sharing between the two countries, but maintained the US had intentionally throttled its Starlink satellite internet access to send a “message” to Kyiv, write Andrew Roth and Sam Jones.

Lithuania said Russia was likely behind an attempted arson attack on a company hosting communication hardware for Starlink satellites. Prime minister Mindaugas Sinkevicius made the claim on broadcaster LRT after authorities discovered flammable liquids at the company in question. Sinkevicius said the firm, whose location he did not mention, houses “nine satellite antennas to guarantee the Starlink connection, which of course supports and assists Ukraine”. He added: “It is obvious this is part of the hybrid war being waged by Russia, involving acts of sabotage.”

In September, a satellite station belonging to the network located in central Poland was set ablaze with Warsaw claiming sabotage. In Bulgaria, an investigation is under way amid claims that antennas linked to the Starlink satellite network were set on fire.

Shipping Russian diesel to the US market will take 15 to 20 days once contracts are signed, a senior Russian official said on Sunday, though a date for signing has yet to be announced. Trump announced the controversial agreement with Moscow last week, seen as a way to try to lower fuel prices for American consumers ahead of crucial midterm elections. “Negotiations are currently under way regarding the commercial terms – that is, on finalisation of the contracts,” Russian deputy prime minister for energy Alexander Novak said in an interview with state media. “Once the contracts are signed, the fuel will reach the markets – in this case, the US markets – within 15 to 20 days.”

Ukrainian strikes set an oil export terminal and a depot ablaze in St Petersburg on Sunday as Kyiv launched more than 1,000 drones at Russia in one of its largest aerial attacks of the war. One person was killed and five others were wounded in the attack, which sparked fires at the Petersburg oil terminal and the city’s Ruchi oil depot, officials said. A logistics centre belonging to Russian retailer Ozon and a datacentre operated by Russian tech company VK were also targeted, the companies confirmed. Russia’s defence ministry said Sunday that its forces had destroyed 1,015 Ukrainian drones over 15 Russian regions, the annexed Ukrainian peninsula of Crimea and the Black Sea.

A ⁠Russian air ⁠strike ⁠killed one person ​and injured ⁠two in Kyiv ‌overnight, mayor Vitali ‌Klitschko said on Telegram early on ‌Monday. A medical facility ​and a non-residential ⁠building were damaged ​in the ​attack, ​he ​said.

A suspected ⁠drone exploded over Lithuania after triggering an alert that forced residents in northern and central areas to seek shelter for an hour on Sunday, officials said. Ukraine’s foreign ​ministry said later it regretted the incident in Lithuania’s airspace, adding that it may have resulted from Russian electronic warfare diverting drones off course. The object flew ⁠into Lithuania’s airspace from Poland, Lithuanian defence minister Robertas Kaunas told reporters.

item.title: Nationwide meat recall underway as ‘temperature abuse’ impacts 1.5 million pounds of beef, pork, and chicken
item.description:
A massive recall involving more than 1.5 million pounds of meat product was announced this weekend after the manufacturer discovered what the U.S. Department of Agriculture’s Food Safety and Inspection Service (FSIS) deemed to be possible “temperature abuse.”

Here’s what that means, what meat products are affected, and what you should do if you have any of the recalled items.

What’s happened?

On Saturday, the USDA’s Food Safety and Inspection Service alerted the public about a voluntary recall by Kayem Foods Inc., a more-than-a-century-old meat products company based in Chelsea, Massachusetts.

The recall involves more than 1.5 million pounds of meat products produced by Kayem Foods. According to the FSIS, Kayem is recalling 1,584,361 pounds of ready-to-eat (RTE) meat and poultry products over fears that impacted products “may have experienced temperature abuse during storage.”

The problem was discovered after one of Kayem Foods’ retail customers complained about warm product temperatures related to some of the meat products, the notice states.

Kayem then investigated the claims and found one of the warehouse coolers where the products were stored “experienced temperature deviations,” according to the FSIS.

What is “temperature abuse”?

While the term “temperature abuse” makes it sound like someone knowingly altered the meats’ temperature, the situation is actually less nefarious.

In relation to this recall, “temperature abuse” simply means that the products’ temperatures deviated from what they should have been stored at, potentially making the products unsafe to eat.

In a recall notice posted directly on Kayem Foods’ website, the company says that the issue was due to “a cooling system malfunction at one of the company’s warehouses that resulted in storage temperature deviations.” 

Announcing the recall, Kayem CEO Matt Monkiewicz said, “Our business depends on providing consumers with safe food of the highest quality. Out of an abundance of caution, we are undertaking this voluntary recall.”

He added: “We take food safety very seriously and apologize to our valued consumers. Our management team takes full responsibility. We have learned from and corrected the issue and will not allow this to happen again.” 

What products are included in the recall?

The more than 1.5 million pounds of meat products impacted by the recall include items sold under nine different brands:

  • Al Fresco
  • Deutschmacher
  • Essem
  • Genoa
  • Jordan’s
  • Kayem
  • McKenzie
  • Triple M
  • Winnisimmet

The products include numerous ready-to-eat items, such as sausages, chicken, pork, bacon, and other products. 

The FSIS says the recalled products bear the establishment numbers “EST. M/P 7839,” “EST. P 20935A” and “EST. M 9520” inside the USDA mark of inspection.

Items included in the recall “were produced approximately March 31, 2026, to Oct. 7, 2026.” Kayem Foods says the items were “stored and shipped between June 7, 2026, and October 14, 2026.”

The FSIS has published a full list of the items on its website. The agency has also published photos of the product packaging.

Kayem Foods has published its own list of recalled items here.

Where were the recalled products sold?

Neither the FSIS nor Kayem Foods has announced which retailers sold the recalled products. However, the FSIS says that the “items were shipped to retail and foodservice locations Nationwide and Hong Kong.”

The agency says that, as of the time of its notification, there have been no confirmed reports of anyone becoming ill from eating the recalled items.

What should I do if I have the recalled products?

The FSIS says consumers should check their refrigerators, as the items could still reside there even if purchased long ago. 

Consumers who have the recalled items are being urged not to consume them, but instead dispose of them or return them to their place of purchase.

Those with questions about the recall can contact Kayem Foods Customer Service at 800-426-6100 or email the company at info@kayem.com.

item.title: Ukraine war briefing: Zelenskyy claims US deliberately delaying interceptor missile deliveries to Kyiv
item.description:
Ukrainian president tells US senators the delayed missiles have already been paid for by European countries, amid growing rift. What we know on day 1,700

Volodymyr Zelenskyy has said the US is deliberately delaying deliveries of interceptor missiles to Ukraine, deepening a public spat with Donald Trump. Speaking to US senators on Monday, the Ukrainian president claimed that “the Pentagon is delaying the delivery of missiles” already paid for by European countries under the prioritised Ukraine requirements list (Purl) program. According to Zelenskyy, the shipment is awaiting the signature of the US defence secretary, Pete Hegseth. A White House official, who spoke to the Washington Post on the condition of anonymity to discuss sensitive diplomacy, said the US “continues to play a constructive role in speaking to both sides in working towards bringing the war to an end”.

Zelenskyy also said several European countries were ready to transfer Patriot interceptor missiles from their own stockpiles but were still awaiting US approval. “All of this suggests that some political decision has been made to slow down the support for us,” he said in remarks released by the Ukrainian presidency. The ‌Post reported the Trump ⁠administration ​had not approved ⁠the ⁠transfer of the interceptor ‌missiles ‌to Ukraine.

Trump has blamed Ukrainian strikes on Russian oil refineries for soaring fuel prices that are a major issue in coming US midterm elections. “Maybe it’s time for ​Zelenskyy ‌to get ‌somebody else to negotiate” to end the war with Russia, Trump said on Monday. Zelenskyy said US decisions taken ⁠on the war – including delays in arms shipments and restrictions on ⁠intelligence sharing – were “hard ⁠to explain”. Washington denies making any changes to intelligence-sharing with Kyiv.

Ukraine did not receive a warning from the US about an impending Russian missile attack on Sunday evening, Zelenskyy said, reviving concerns that Washington is withholding intelligence to bully Kyiv into capitulating to Moscow. Ukrainian air force spokesperson Yuri Ihnat said on Monday morning that Ukraine had not received a warning before a Russian missile barrage hit power plants in Kyiv about 11pm, Andrew Roth reports. Earlier, a Ukrainian government official had told the Guardian the US had not warned the capital about the impending missile strike. Ukraine did receive a warning before a subsequent strike, Ihnat added. Zelenskyy said on social media on Monday morning: “Once again, Russia launched a ballistic missile attack in multiple waves throughout the night, and once again, there was no warning from our partners.”

Six people, including young children, were killed when a Russian drone struck a park in Ukraine’s north-eastern Kharkiv region, authorities said. Zelenskyy decried a “pure atrocity”, saying on Facebook the drone “struck people directly – in a park near an ordinary cafe”, and a one-year-old girl was among those killed. The strike on Monday in Nova Vodolaga had also killed the girl’s mother.

Trump’s ⁠envoy Steve Witkoff is ⁠set to travel to Norway ​this week for the next round of negotiations on ending the war in Ukraine, Reuters quoted three people familiar with the matter as saying. Two of them said they expected Zelenskyy to ⁠attend the meetings. Another source said Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner, who was expected to take part in the talks, was sick and would attend virtually. The Oslo discussions were expected to include Zelenskyy, Norwegian prime ⁠minister Jonas Gahr Store, representatives of the E4 – made up of the UK, France, Germany and Poland – the EU and Nato. item.title: Salesforce is planning to buy AI marketing company Braze, sending BRZE shares surging 50%
item.description:
A move announced by the software-as-a-service giant Salesforce (NYSE: CRM) is sending the stock price of a relatively unknown AI marketing firm surging this morning. Here’s what you need to know.

What’s happened?

On Tuesday morning, Salesforce announced plans to acquire digital marketing firm Braze (Nasdaq: BRZE) for about $5.66 billion. According to the terms of the deal, Salesforce will pay Braze Class A common stockholders $47.50 in cash per share. 

Braze’s AI-powered multichannel marketing solutions will be integrated into Salesforce’s core offerings, which Salesforce believes will give it an edge with its enterprise solutions.

This is especially true at a time when Wall Street has become concerned about a so-called SaaSpocalypse. Business models of legacy software-as-a-service companies are feared to be under threat as businesses increasingly turn to AI solutions to meet their needs.

“AI is raising the bar for marketers, who now need agentic solutions that can understand customers, make decisions, and act in real time,” Salesforce noted in a release announcing the news, adding that “Braze’s real-time engagement and AI decisioning capabilities are expected to complement all four layers of Salesforce’s architecture — Data 360, Customer 360, Agentforce, and SIForce.”

What is Braze?

While even those outside the tech industry have likely heard of Salesforce, Braze is a much smaller and lesser-known company.

It is headquartered in New York and was originally founded in 2011. Its primary focus is as a multichannel marketing provider for enterprise customers to help them better understand and interact with their consumers.

Braze allows companies to interact with their customers across multiple channels, including WhatsApp, email, mobile websites, and more. In recent years, the company has shifted to AI offerings to better help clients engage with their customers.

Braze currently says it has around 2,770 customers, which include Venmo, Dairy Queen, Instacart, Canva, and more.

The company was private for the first decade of its existence, but went public in 2021 on the Nasdaq.

Braze shares skyrocket 50% 

Salesforce’s offer price of $5.66 billion for Braze equates to about a 58% premium over what the company was valued at as of market close yesterday, when BRZE shares closed just above $30.

Given that premium, it’s no wonder that BRZE skyrocketed right after the deal was announced. Currently, as of the time of this writing, BRZE shares are up more than 50% to $45.33 per share. That’s just a little more than $2 below what Salesforce says it will pay for the company.

Still, the stock’s current price is a far cry from its 2021 post-IPO highs.

Shortly after Braze went public, its shares traded at almost $100 per share at one point, according to Yahoo Finance data. But since then—even with today’s 50% gains—BRZE shares have fallen by around 48%.

Of course, while Salesforce has announced its intentions to buy the company, no deal of this size is certain until regulators have signed off and money has actually exchanged hands. And that won’t be during Salesforce’s current fiscal year.

Salesforce says the deal is expected to close during the company’s 2028 fiscal year, which runs from February 1, 2027, to January 31, 2028. It did not give an indication of when during that fiscal year the sale would close.

item.title: U.S. bans AI startup DeepSeek because of ‘threat vectors’ and China responds
item.description:
China hit back Tuesday at a U.S. ban on Chinese artificial intelligence startup DeepSeek’s products for federal civilian agencies, highlighting friction in the two AI powers’ heated technology race.

The agencies should remove DeepSeek and its affiliated products, as well as third party products and services developed using DeepSeek, from their IT systems, the Department of Homeland Security said in a notice made public on Monday.

The department’s order, dating back to late July, also blocks civilian agencies from procuring DeepSeek products and services. DeepSeek is one of China’s leading and best-known AI companies and its open-source models are widely available in countries including the United States. They are mostly free to use.

The notice in the Federal Register alleges that DeepSeek’s models “present multiple threat vectors.” It said concerns include that its servers are located in China and that Chinese authorities’ could potentially access private company infrastructure and sensitive U.S. data.

In Beijing, Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson Mao Ning said China will “will resolutely safeguard the legitimate rights and interests of Chinese companies” when asked at a regular press conference about the U.S. ban.

“China consistently opposes the overstretching of the concept of national security and the politicizing of science, technology, economic and trade issues,” she told reporters at a routine briefing.

DeepSeek did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

U.S. President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping are set to meet in mid-November on the sidelines of the APEC, or Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation, leaders’ summit in Shenzhen, China.

AI is expected to be on the agenda.

China and the U.S. have recently made progress in some collaboration on AI governance, including a U.S. proposal for setting up of a notification system on national security-related incidents, but the two countries are still at odds on many issues.

U.S.-led restrictions still ban China from accessing some of the world’s most advanced AI chips and the machines that make them. Last week, Beijing rolled out new proposed plans to restrict exports of certain advanced AI models.

The U.S. has also said Chinese AI startups including DeepSeek engaged in large-scale “distillation,” or extraction of capabilities, from frontier American AI models, claims that Beijing has dismissed.

Earlier this year, the U.S. Federal Communications Commission announced it was barring imports of new foreign-made humanoid robots in a move seen as targeting China.

—Chan Ho-Him, AP Business Writer

Zelenskyy travelled to Oslo seeking to repair relations with Washington, which have sunk to new lows. Trump’s recent gestures toward Moscow, including a deal to buy Russian diesel and a waiver of new sanctions, have sparked bipartisan pushback in the US Congress and worry in European capitals. item.title: The UN’s latest climate change report is spotlighting the U.S., and not for a good reason
item.description:
Losing more ground in the fight against climate change, humanity is heading for a hotter world than experts projected last year — and the United States is a big reason for that, a new United Nations report says.

If all the countries do what they promise to reduce heat-trapping emissions, Earth will likely still warm another 2.2 degrees Fahrenheit (1.2 degrees Celsius) above current temperatures, according to Wednesday’s update of climate calculations by the United Nations Environment Programme. That’s about two-tenths of a degree Fahrenheit (0.1 degrees Celsius) more than last year’s projections by the same science team.

“This is a worse outcome than expected last year, as a result of the formal withdrawal of the United States of America from the Paris Agreement and revised estimates of historical emissions,” the report said. The report also blames the United States for increased emissions last year, saying all the other top 20 major economies reduced their carbon pollution or at least slowed the growth in how much carbon dioxide was spewed from the burning of coal, oil and gas.

“In terms of magnitude, the increase in the United States of America (133 megatons of CO2 equivalent) far exceeded that of all other countries and was driven by increased electricity demand and a rebound of coal power generation,” the report said. The 124 countries that increased emissions — not counting the 63 that decreased like most European nations — added 189 million tons of carbon dioxide in 2025, and 70% of that increase came from the U.S., according to the report.

The United States is going “hell-for-leather trying to block renewables while actively promoting and subsidizing dirty coal — and its diplomacy is trying to make other countries also pull back on action. It is looking at the fire, denying there is a fire, and then pouring more petrol on it,” said Australian climate scientist Bill Hare, CEO of Climate Analytics that measures countries’ climate fighting plans. He wasn’t part of the U.N. report but like several other outside scientists said it was scientifically sound.

Shooting far past Paris climate goal

The new calculations say that if countries do all they promise in the climate fighting plans they submitted to the United Nations, by 2100 the globe will be 2.6 degrees Celsius (4.7 degrees Fahrenheit) hotter than pre-industrial times. If the world continues on its current path — without national promises — it will be 2.8 degrees Celsius (5 degrees Fahrenheit) warmer than the last half of the 19th century, the same as last year’s projection.

Both of those temperatures blow far past the goal of less than 2 degrees Celsius (3.6 degrees Fahrenheit) and preferably 1.5 degrees Celsius (2.7 degrees Fahrenheit) adopted by the 2015 Paris climate pact. The world is now at about 1.4 degrees Celsius (2.5 degrees Fahrenheit) above pre-industrial times and earlier this year — and again in this report — United Nations officials conceded that there is no way of limiting warming to the 1.5-degree goal that they had embraced. Instead, officials are pinning their hopes of limiting warming to about 1.8 degrees Celsius (3.2 degrees Fahrenheit) and then somehow pulling enough carbon dioxide out of the air to lower temperatures back down to 1.5 degrees.

The world is falling “dangerously short” of even those goals, United Nations Secretary-General António Guterres said, “but we have the tools to change course and pull back from the brink.”

Drastically cutting global carbon emissions — by 18% by 2030 and 69% by 2040 — “is the only way that we can get back to a semblance of a reality that is still largely manageable without major impacts and therefore that makes every sense,” said UNEP Executive Director Inger Andersen.

“The report’s message is clear,” said climate scientist Adelle Thomas, vice chair of a United Nations scientific assessment on climate impacts. She wasn’t part of this study. “We know what needs to be done. We have the tools to do it. And delay only makes the challenge more dangerous and more expensive for all.”

An added tenth of a degree of danger

Report lead author Anne Olhoff, director of UNEP Copenhagen Climate Centre, said the U.S. policy change will likely add one-tenth of a degree Celsius (nearly two-tenths of a degree Fahrenheit) to global temperatures by the end of the century.

“This report shows that America’s retreat isn’t just a political embarrassment. It has real consequences for the planet and for millions of people around the world,” said Mohamed Adow, director of Power Shift Africa, a climate organization. “An extra tenth of a degree might sound insignificant, but in climate terms it is enormous. It means more dangerous heat waves, more destructive floods, more failed harvests and more lives lost. For vulnerable communities in Africa, already living on the front lines of the climate crisis, every fraction of a degree matters. These are not abstract numbers. They are human lives.”

Hare said that extra one-tenth of a degree pushes an additional 140 million people “into dangerously hot conditions” and increases the odds of the collapse of the Amazon rain forest or ice sheets in Greenland and Antarctica. It also would cost the world and shave about $1.2 trillion from the global economy, said University of Pennsylvania climate scientist Michael Mann.

And the U.S. effect is probably even bigger than what the United Nations calculates because if the world’s largest historical climate polluter doesn’t do much to fight global warming other nations ease off in their efforts too, said Johan Rockstrom, director of the Potsdam Institute for Climate Impacts Research in Germany.

“The rest of the world is exhausted when it comes to counting the damage that the U.S. is willingly doing to allies, multilateral structures, economic cooperation, disaster relief,” Australian climate scientist Malte Meinshausen said. “The rest of the world should probably continue to focus even less on the U.S.”

—Seth Borenstein, AP Science Writer

item.title: BBC layoffs: More jobs slashed, channels cut as British broadcaster faces ‘immediate cost pressures’
item.description:
Media companies continue to struggle as consumers pivot away from traditional forms of content. 

The latest example comes from the BBC, which has announced it will cut over 100 jobs. The U.K.-based broadcaster is attempting to save £500 million ($670 million) over the next two years. 

BBC is primarily funded by a licensing fee, a £180 annual payment that provides viewers with all TV channels, streaming services, and more. It’s designed to keep the BBC “free of advertisements and independent of shareholder and political interest” in the U.K. 

However, the number of TV licenses sold has shrunk in recent years. 

“We need to make every pound work harder for audiences as we respond to the immediate cost pressures and reinvent the BBC for a changing world,” BBC director-general Matt Brittin said in a statement. “We all know that means tough choices.” 

Channels and archive radio network cut

In pursuit of this mission, the BBC will also stop broadcasting BBC Scotland and BBC Three, a channel geared toward younger audiences, come spring. It’s further cutting archive radio network Radio 4 Extra, with its content available on the BBC Sounds app. 

“Axing these TV channels and Radio 4 Extra may make business sense in a world where audiences are increasingly finding their BBC content on-demand, but I understand it saves less than 10 million pounds a year, a tiny fraction of what’s needed,” BBC News culture and media editor Katie Razzall said in a broadcast. “So far, the BBC has announced 200 million pounds in savings; it needs to find another 300 million pounds more.” 

The BBC plans to cut between 1,800 and 2,000 jobs over the next couple years. It already slashed 550 positions in June. 

“There is a bigger fight going on here,” Razzall elaborated in an article. “The BBC is negotiating with the government over its future—and how it will be paid for. It won’t harm the negotiations if it can show the corporation is being streamlined and made more efficient.” 

Rachel Jupp, director of BBC News, will be announcing more savings plans in early 2027. 

Reached for comment, a BBC spokesperson referred Fast Company to its press release about the latest cuts.

BBC Three commissioned popular shows such as Fleabag, Killing Eve, and Normal People. Despite cutting its broadcast, the BBC Three team is receiving more money for commissions targeting audiences aged 16 to 34. 

BBC Scotland and BBC Three will be available on BBC iPlayer, the company’s online streamer, along with other platforms such as YouTube. BBC Scotland’s programs will also air on BBC One or BBC Two in the country, but the channel’s nightly News at Seven will stop running. According to the BBC, 12% of Scots watched BBC Scotland last year.

item.title: Netflix’s stock just collapsed to a 2-year low: Is the streaming giant’s ad business in trouble?
item.description:
Shares in Netflix Inc. (Nasdaq: NFLX) have fallen to a more than a two-year low after the streaming giant posted its Q3 2026 results yesterday.

Despite hitting Wall Street’s projected revenue target of nearly $12.9 billion for the quarter, an update on the company’s increasingly critical ad business dampened investor optimism, sinking the stock with it. Here’s what you need to know.

What’s happened?

Yesterday, Netflix announced its results for its third quarter of fiscal 2026. Unfortunately for the company, those results—and Netflix’s guidance—were somewhat of a mixed bag.

There was good news: Revenue for the quarter totaled $12.87 billion, representing 11.8% year-over-year growth.

The company’s diluted earnings per share also reached 87 cents. As noted by CNBC, this means Netflix hit the revenue target investors were expecting and exceeded EPS expectations by five cents per share.

However, there was also plenty of news that gave investors pause—and that has caused the stock to drop significantly in premarket trading today.

What did Netflix project?

For the fourth quarter, Netflix said it expects revenue to grow by about 11.5% to $13.44 billion. Double-digit growth is nothing to sneeze at, but unfortunately for Netflix, that revenue forecast comes in under the $13.51 billion that Wall Street was expecting, notes TipRanks. 

When it comes to its full fiscal 2026 guidance, Netflix says it now expects revenue of $51.1 billion. As with its Q4 forecast, that is a double-digit increase (about 13% year over year), but it is also on the lower end of the $51.0 to $51.4 billion range Netflix previously forecast for fiscal 2026.

But perhaps what spooked investors most of all was the updated guidance for Netflix’s ad business. The company said it now expects full-year 2026 ad revenue to be around $2.7 billion. That’s $300 million, or 10% less, than the $3 billion in ad revenue Netflix had previously forecast.

What’s weighing on Netflix’s ad business?

As most Netflix subscribers will have noticed, the company has been raising prices on its ad-free subscriptions for years. But Netflix isn’t stupid. It knows that price rises mean consumers’ pocketbooks will be hit harder.

However, Netflix also believes that by jacking up ad-free subscription costs, it will cause many cost-conscious consumers not to cancel their subscriptions, but instead to opt for lower-cost, ad-supported tiers.

While these lower-priced subscriptions mean Netflix will extract less up-front revenue from subscribers, over the long run, Netflix should make more money from each subscriber by serving them ads.

Netflix isn’t alone in this. Nearly every major streaming service has introduced ad-supported tiers in recent years in hopes of transitioning more users to them in order to boost their bottom lines.

In the industry, ad-supported subscriptions are seen as a way for streamers to boost revenue. Investors, too, have put significant hopes for revenue growth into ad-supported tiers.

That’s why investors were so disheartened to hear Netflix announce that its total full-year 2026 ad revenue is expected to come in 10% lower than previously forecast. 

As for one of the primary causes of the ad forecast reduction, Netflix co-CEO Greg Peters said it was due to a slower launch of some ad products than originally expected.

“[S]pecifically in this case, we’ve seen some delays in the rollout and partner integrations for some of those new ads products,” Peters said on the company’s financial call, according to a PitchBook transcript. “So getting to the integration model that we want sometimes takes a bit more work with our partners, but we strongly believe that a modest short-term hit for a better long-term strategic position is a good ultimate tradeoff.”

Peters added that the slower rollout shouldn’t impact long-term gains, but investors tend to think in quarters, not the long term. And the lower ad forecast helped drive Netflix stock lower as well.

How have NFLX shares reacted?

As of the time of this writing, NFLX shares are down more than 6.4% to $64.23 in premarket trading. That’s after the company’s shares closed down 1.66% yesterday to $68.69.

Netflix’s current premarket price of around $64 per share is an ignominious milestone for the company. Its share price has not been that low since August 2024—more than two years ago. 

Even before today’s 6.4% drop, Netflix’s stock price was trading down more than 26% for the year.

Over the past year, the stock’s price has declined a staggering 44.5% as of yesterday’s close, according to data from Yahoo Finance.

Where the stock goes next is anyone’s guess, but investors will clearly be keeping an eye on the company’s ad efforts in the quarters ahead—efforts Peters seems to have faith in.

“[U]ltimately, advertisers want our new products and features, and that’s a big mechanism of growth for us,” he told analysts on yesterday’s call. “So we are very focused on getting those out to them as quickly as we possibly can.”

Correction: Netflix’s previous 2026 guidance was in the $51.0 to $51.4 billion range, not $15.0 to $15.4 billion range as an earlier version of this article stated.

item.title: 7 oil tankers hit in the Strait of Hormuz reignite fears of returning to full-scale war
item.description:
Seven oil tankers caught fire or were damaged in the Strait of Hormuz overnight after being hit by Iran or striking naval mines, Tehran said Thursday, a markedly high number as tensions rise over concerns about a return to all-out war.

With days before a close election in Israel in which Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu could lose power, and before next month’s U.S. midterm election in which war-linked high prices have sparked voter anger, there are concerns that U.S.-Israeli attacks on Iran could resume.

“Netanyahu wants to attack Iran, that’s not even a question,” Danny Citrinowicz, a researcher at Israel’s Institute for National Security Studies and a former Iran specialist in Israel’s military and intelligence services, told The Associated Press.

He accused Israel of rushing into another round with Iran without revamping its strategy. A clear Netanyahu victory in the Oct. 27 election means an attack is almost guaranteed, he said.

Main opposition candidates are likely to focus on domestic issues first, but Citrinowicz said he believed the region is on the way toward “another kinetic escalation.”

Iran repeats threat to attack U.S. bases in the region

Iranian state television reported the claims about the latest attacks on ships, which the AP couldn’t independently confirm. The report cited the Revolutionary Guard Corps navy, which again threatened to strike U.S. military bases in the region if the U.S. keeps helping to guide commercial ships through the strait.

The report didn’t mention casualties. Iran still asserts control over the waterway, a central point of leverage in any talks with the U.S. over the war.

October has had the most reported attacks on commercial shipping since March in the war’s opening weeks, according to a British military monitor, the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations. UKMTO didn’t report the latest attacks, but it has noted new reluctance by some shippers to report incidents.

Oil producers have found ways to keep crude flowing, experts say, but at a mounting cost.

Tankers continue moving through Strait of Hormuz despite attacks

Oil tankers are still moving oil through the strait under U.S. military protection despite the recent upsurge in attacks, according to shipping data and analysis company Lloyd’s List Intelligence.

Tanker operators willing to risk the voyage have been shuttling oil from Gulf producers through the strait at night with their location systems and mobile phones turned off using a U.S.-protected lane near the coast of Oman. Those tankers transfer oil to other tankers waiting in the Gulf of Oman for shipment to customers in Asia.

Those “active Gulf operators show little sign of retreating” despite 28 attacks on ships in October, the highest since the start of the war, Lloyd’s said in an online webinar Thursday.

The so-called “dark shuttle” overseen by U.S. Central Command has helped keep oil shipments from the Gulf at roughly prewar levels, but at high costs in time, money and sailors’ lives. Spot charter rates for tankers have soared into the hundreds of thousands of dollars a day, while the ship-to-ship transfers can take several days.

Iran says it’s open to diplomacy but also self-defense

Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi on Wednesday said that a wary Tehran remains open to diplomacy, but is ready to defend itself.

Iran has warned that it has learned important military lessons from the war that began with U.S. and Israeli attacks on Feb. 28. In recent days, Tehran has indicated that it could expand targets to include infrastructure such as undersea cables and data centers.

The United States, for its part, is sending more military assets to the region, including a third aircraft carrier and thousands of troops, to join the largest force of American warships and aircraft in the Middle East in decades.

Mediators, meanwhile, have been trying to bring Washington and Tehran back to formal talks.

Iran still promotes its latest proposal that would end the war and fully open the strait within a week if the U.S. meets several conditions. Those conditions, which include ending the U.S. blockade of Iranian ports, echo ones in the deal that fell apart within days of both sides signing it in June.

In late September, U.S. President Donald Trump rejected that seven-day proposal, but both sides have acknowledged that indirect discussions have continued.

The stakes are even higher if all-out war resumes

A return to full fighting would again endanger civilians throughout the region and complicate global deliveries of oil, natural gas, and related products like fertilizer from the region and likely bring another spike in prices.

The head of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council, Mohsen Rezaei, this week acknowledged that the Islamic Republic will suffer under a prolonged U.S. blockade. But economic pain and strategic collapse are not the same thing, he added, according to Iran’s state-run IRNA news agency.

Now the landscape of the conflict has widened with the recent surge in fighting between Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthis and Saudi Arabia. The Saudi kingdom backs a coalition of forces with Yemen’s internationally recognized government that is fighting the rebels.

The Houthis’ repeated deadly attacks on airports and other facilities inside Saudi Arabia have pressured the close U.S. ally, which has sought military aid.

The escalation also has threatened a crucial shipping corridor, the Bab el-Mandeb at the southern end of the Red Sea.

—Melanie Lidman, Associated Press

item.title: Barclays layoffs today: Bank slashes 5% of workforce, attributing 5,000 job cuts to AI
item.description:
The layoffs just keep coming: Barclays announced it is slashing 5,000 jobs, or about 5% of its workforce. It’s attributing the cuts to artificial intelligence, which the bank says has made its operations more efficient.

Of the 5,000 job cuts, 1,000 of the positions have already been eliminated, with another 4,000 layoffs scheduled by the end of this year. Many of those jobs are in developer and support roles.

As Fast Company recently reported, the AI Industry Exposure index, which identifies which industries are most exposed to potential AI disruption—i.e., job loss—found workers in finance and insurance had some of the highest levels of exposure.

“We are positioning Barclays for the future, building the workforce and skills needed to deliver our strategy and meet the evolving needs of our customers and clients,” a Barclays spokesperson told Fast Company in a statement. “This includes investing £150m in our colleagues’ future skills by 2030, with 40,000 colleagues having already accessed our AI learning, which is available to all. For those who may be impacted by these changes, we provide a tailored career support and coaching service.”

The cuts will mainly affect the company’s U.K. retail banking operation, which is heavily staffed in India, where a large number of positions are expected to be eliminated, according to the BBC.

The bank, which is headquartered in the U.K. but operates globally, reported third-quarter earnings on Thursday. For the three-month period ending September 30, it reported pre-tax profits of £2.3 billion ($3 billion), up 12% from the same period last year, but missed analyst expectations of £2.42 billion.

Barclays joins a long list of banks and other companies that have announced layoffs this year in the name of AI efficiency. Those include but are not limited to: Citigroup, which is eliminating up to 20,000 jobs, or 10% of its workforce; HSBC, which reportedly cleared out 10% of its highly-paid senior bankers; and Standard Chartered, which is cutting 7,000 jobs, or 15% of corporate function roles, by 2030.

AI stocks slip and global markets retreat as oil hits 5-month high
item.description:
Drops for stocks in the artificial-intelligence industry are dragging markets down worldwide on Thursday, while oil prices hit their highest levels since May on worries about the war with Iran.

The S&P 500 sank 1.3% following even sharper losses in Asia, whose markets are full of AI and other technology stocks. The Nasdaq composite was down 2.4%, as of 12:56 p.m. ET, but stocks outside of tech did better, and the Dow Jones Industrial Average was down a more modest 40 points, or 0.1%.

AI-related stocks have been shaky on worries that their boom may be under threat because of how expensive it’s become to borrow money to build data centers and buy more AI chips. Concerns also remain that stock prices simply shot too high in their yearslong frenzy, even though companies in the industry continue to report growth.

Lam Research, whose equipment and services help make semiconductors, reported gains in profit and revenue for the summer that were slightly stronger than analysts expected, for example. Usually, that helps boost a stock’s price, but Lam Research’s tumbled 11.1%.

It gave a range for its forecast for profit this quarter whose midpoint was slightly below analysts’ expectations. Its stock also came into the day with a 52.4% surge for the year so far, nearly quadruple the already healthy gain for the overall S&P 500, leaving plenty of room for potential disappointment.

Other big tech stocks were unsettled following their own quarterly reports that included at least some encouraging nuggets.

Meta Platforms, which is pushing its Muse AI agent, lost 7.4% after reporting stronger revenue for the latest quarter than analysts expected, though its profit fell short. The company behind Facebook and Instagram also said it’s creating a new class of stock to raise money to pay for AI investments and other expenses.

Tesla slipped 2.1% after flipping between gains and losses in the morning. It reported a stronger profit for the summer than analysts expected, though its revenue was weaker than forecast.

The global tide against AI stocks knocked Nvidia down 4.3%. Because it’s the largest stock on Wall Street by total value, the chip giant was the heaviest weight on the S&P 500.

CoreWeave, which has borrowed money to buy Nvidia’s AI chips that it rents out to customers over the cloud, has been particularly shaky in recent weeks because of worries about its debt. It dropped 9.6%, though it’s swung between wide gains and losses of roughly 4% within each of the last two days.

The weakness for AI and other tech stocks began in Asia, where South Korea’s Kospi tumbled 3.5%, Hong Kong’s Hang Seng dropped 3%, and Japan’s Nikkei 225 sank 2.7%.

Also weighing on global stock markets was a jump in oil prices.

The price for a barrel of Brent crude oil rose 2.9% to $111.99 after touching its highest level in five months. It’s at the high end of the $97 to $112 range it’s been yo-yoing through in October on uncertainty about when the war with Iran will allow the global energy industry to return to normal.

In Europe, France’s CAC 40 stock index fell to one of the continent’s sharpest losses with a drop of 1.4%. It has fewer tech stocks than Asian or U.S. indexes, but it was hurt by another jump in yields for French government bonds.

Yields have been generally climbing there because of worries about the government’s big debt load and strained budget. Violent protests across France have raised pressure on the government to increase spending, which could add further to its debt.

Worries about big government debt are weighing on almost every developed economy in the world, including the United States. Such concerns have pushed yields in the U.S. bond market to their highest levels in decades, along with high inflation, signals of a still-strong U.S. economy and other factors.

But U.S. yields nevertheless fell sharply Thursday in a signal that investors were buying U.S. government bonds in search of something safer to own as AI stocks tumbled.

The yield on the 10-year Treasury fell to 4.98% from 5.13% late Wednesday and from more than 5.30% earlier this month. That’s a major move for the bond market, though the 10-year yield remains well above its 3.97% level from before the war with Iran.

Thursday’s drop in yields came even as another report suggested the U.S. economy may be doing better than economists expected. It said fewer U.S. workers applied for unemployment benefits last week, which could signal that layoffs remain low across the country.

That solid economy has helped U.S. companies broadly to make bigger profits, which is what propelled the U.S. stock market to a record high earlier this month despite the many worries tugging at it. The majority of stocks within the S&P 500 rose on Thursday, only to get drowned out by the drops for more influential tech stocks.

Procter & Gamble, Lockheed Martin, and CSX were among the latest companies to join the list of those topping profit expectations for the summer, and gains for their stocks helped limit the market’s losses on Thursday.

CEO Shailesh Jejurikar said Procter & Gamble expects “geopolitical and economic challenges” to continue, but it stood by its forecasts for growth in revenue, profit, and other measures for the full year. The stock price for the company behind the Crest, Olay and Oral-B brands rose 6.3%.

—By Stan Choe, AP business writer

item.title: The U.S. Treasury wants expanded restrictions on high-tech investments to these ‘countries of concern’
item.description:
The U.S. Treasury Department proposed a rule Thursday to crack down on American high-tech investments such as supercomputing and artificial intelligence in China, Russia, North Korea and other “countries of concern.”

The U.S. government has been working for years to deny China and other adversaries investments that could help them boost their military power.

That program began in 2023 when then-President Joe Biden signed an executive order putting restrictions on outbound U.S. investments in sectors such as semiconductors, quantum computing and artificial intelligence going into China. Treasury later established the Outbound Investment Security Program.

In December 2025, Congress passed a law that codified and expanded the program to target more technologies and more foreign countries, including Cuba, Iran, North Korea and Russia.

The inclusion of Russia in the proposed rule has come days after President Donald Trump waived sanctions on Russia following a diesel deal with President Vladimir Putin.

The rule announced Thursday would expand the restrictions to cover investments in hypersonic systems capable of traveling at five times the speed of sound, supercomputing, biotechnology and artificial intelligence, though Treasury used Trump’s favored term for AI, “superintelligence” or SI.

The proposed rule “sends an important signal to markets that Washington is tracking where U.S. capital is flowing and what capabilities it is helping build,” said Craig Singleton, a senior fellow at the think tank Foundation for Defense of Democracies.

The screening of outbound investments “recognizes that capital can accelerate military-relevant capabilities just as surely as technology transfer can,” Singleton said.

Jason Chipman, a former Justice Department lawyer who specializes in cybersecurity, investment rules and export controls as a partner at the law firm WilmerHale, said the new rule “will require more substantial compliance programs to manage risk.”

Treasury’s rule to implement the 2025 law — the Comprehensive Outbound Investment National Security Act — would only apply to investments that exceed $50,000 and would exclude many financial investments, including stock purchases.

Treasury will hear public comments on the proposal before issuing a final rule.

“It’s just the first step in a fairly long process to get to changes which presumably will be more enforcement-minded, to put more teeth behind the outbound investment program,” said former U.S. trade official Ryan Majerus, now a partner at King & Spalding law firm.

In Beijing, the Chinese Foreign Ministry said the U.S. should abide by the principles of a market economy and stop interfering in normal economic and trade cooperation between businesses.

Asked about Washington’s proposal to add biotechnology to the list, ministry spokesperson Mao Ning said that “Overstretching the concept of national security, taking discriminatory measures against specific countries, and artificially restricting trade, economic and investment activities serve no one’s interests.”

She added that China will closely monitor relevant developments and take necessary measures to safeguard its interests.

Since Trump’s first term, the United States and China — the world’s two biggest economies — have been locked in an economic and tech rivalry. They’ve restricted the export of sensitive technology and critical products — such as China’s rare earth minerals and America’s advanced computer chips — to each other and slapped tariffs on each other’s products. Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping agreed last year to ease tensions while they engaged in talks, a temporary truce they last month extended into January.

But the sparring continues. In July, the Treasury Department issued a $200,000 fine against a U.S.-based company for failing to report to the department a $92,500 investment in a Chinese artificial intelligence and robotics company by one of its subsidiaries.

—Paul Wiseman and Didi Tang, Associated Press

item.title: American Express layoffs: Thousands of roles slashed in AI push as job losses in financial services pile up
item.description:
It hasn’t been a good week for workers in the banking and financial sector. Yesterday, UK banking giant Barclays announced it was laying off 5% of its workforce, or nearly 5,000 workers, as it transitions more of the bank’s operations to artificial intelligence systems.

Across the Atlantic this morning, an American financial giant made a similar announcement.

The American Express Company (NYSE: AXP), owner of the eponymous credit card and associated financial services, announced that it will slash 5% of its workforce due to AI. Here’s what you need to know.

What’s happened?

On Friday morning, American Express CEO Stephen Squeri announced that the U.S. financial giant was eliminating 5% of its global workforce.

American Express had roughly 76,800 employees at the end of 2025, so a 5% reduction equates to about 3,840 job losses.

Amex confirmed the layoffs to Fast Company when reached for comment.

“We’ve got good momentum, but to accelerate innovation and win over the next few years, we need to become a more agile and efficient organization,” American Express CEO Steve Squeri said on a call this morning with analysts.

Squeri added: “When completed, we believe this exercise will help us operate and execute more effectively and give us greater capacity to invest in our business priorities.”

And yes, artificial intelligence is one of the facets driving the layoffs.

American Express chief financial officer Christophe Le Caillec told CNBC that the restructuring in part would help the company “to prepare for AI.”

“You don’t want to automate processes that are not optimally structured, and so what we’re doing here is to reduce layers and increase spans of controls, so that we can automate and take advantage of AI in the coming quarters and the coming years,” Le Caillec told the network.

American Express stock falls

Following the layoff news, American Express’s stock price fell—but likely not because the company announced layoffs. 

Despite the harm to the individual losing their jobs, Wall Street generally cheers job cuts because they are the fastest way for companies to reduce spending and thus increase their bottom line.

The cuts were announced alongside Amex’s Q3 2026 results today. Those results saw the financial giant report record third-quarter revenue of $20.1 billion, which was up 9% year-over-year. Net income reached $3.7 billion, up from $2.9 billion a year earlier.

Yet the company’s stock price is currently trading down around 3% in early morning trading, likely related to a general fall in markets as Brent crude reaches a six-month high amid the ongoing U.S. conflict with Iran.

Year to date, AXP has now fallen around 13%.

As Fast Company reported yesterday, Barclays—and now American Express—are not the only banking giants that have cut jobs in 2026.

Both Citigroup and HSBC cut 10% of their workforces earlier this year. Standard Chartered said it will cut 15% of its workforce by 2030.

item.title: Europe’s brutally hot summer led to more than 50,000 heat deaths in urban areas alone
item.description:
The summer of 2026 was brutally hot across Europe, with five successive heat waves causing record-high temperatures across the continent. 

Those extremes likely led to more than 50,000 excess deaths in urban areas alone, according to a new estimate.

And some 32,000 of those deaths, or nearly two-thirds of that total, can be directly attributed to climate change, caused by the burning of fossil fuels.

This makes the summer of 2026 likely the “worst on record” for heat-related deaths across much of Europe, according to Clair Barnes, a study author and extreme weather and climate change researcher at Imperial College London.

Dangers of extreme heat

The figures come from two recent studies published in the journal Nature Health.

Researchers from Imperial College London and the London School of Hygiene & Tropical Medicine looked at 854 urban areas across 30 countries (27 of which are in the European Union, plus the UK, Norway and Switzerland). Those areas account for 40% of those countries’ total population. 

By using temperature records combined with climate modeling, they were able to estimate how many excess heat-related deaths occurred every summer between 2000 and 2026. Where governments have released official mortality statistics, these findings align with official figures, the researchers say.

Heat death can be difficult to measure. Heat itself often isn’t listed as a cause of death on death certificates, except in certain instances of heat stroke.

But only counting heat strokes is a “vast underestimation of the actual effect” of extreme heat, says Garyfallos Konstantinoudis, a study author and assistant professor at Imperial College London. 

Heat is one of the deadliest climate change impacts. Extreme heat stresses our cardiovascular and metabolic systems, and can combine with other illnesses to exacerbate health harms. 

This is why this count of excess deaths is an estimate, the researchers note. For the summer of 2026, many countries haven’t yet released their official mortality numbers.

Where they have, though, the researchers’ model estimates align with those figures. The researchers estimated, for example, that May and June heat waves in England and Wales caused more than 2,700 deaths. An analysis by the UK Health Security Agency later identified about 2,880 deaths in that time period. 

The role of climate change

The studies also specifically looked at the role of climate change in these deaths by modeling a pre-industrial world in which human-caused climate change didn’t happen.

Even in that world, temperatures were so dangerously hot that they led to high deaths, Barnes says. 

“But that mortality has been pushed substantially higher by human-caused warming, primarily from the burning of fossil fuels,” she adds. “Across Europe as a whole, around two thirds of those deaths would not have occurred without the additional heat from human activity.” 

Temperatures for that entire summer were 2.9°C above the prior decade’s average. Some days were so hot that they hit 12°C above average. 

The summer of 2026 saw the highest number of urban heat deaths in all 26 years the researchers analyzed. The summer of 2022, which was also marred by multiple dangerous heat waves, was second, with about 29,000 deaths. 

Climate change is warming the entire planet, but Europe is the fastest-warming continent. Over the summer, multiple European governments issued “red weather warnings” about the heat, even closing schools and canceling sports events. 

“These numbers are a stark reminder that our hotter, more extreme summers are having an increasingly severe impact on public health. Behind these statistics are real people whose lives were lost and real families who grieve for them,” Barnes says. 

And they’re also a reminder, she adds, “of the growing need to rapidly transition away from fossil fuels to slow the pace of change and limit future warming.”

item.title: Ukraine war briefing: Russian diesel tankers headed for North America, says Moscow, as US tries to revive peace talks
item.description:
Tankers part of US-Russia deal that could see 500,000 metric tonnes of fuel supplied to world market this month. What we know on day 1,704

Three tankers carrying Russian diesel are on their ⁠way to North America, Russian deputy prime minister Alexander Novak said ⁠on Friday. In ​a statement quoted by Russian news agencies, Novak said the cargoes were ⁠part of a deal that could see Russian companies supply 500,000 metric tonnes to US and world markets in October. “The first ⁠three fuel tankers are already on their ​way to the eastern ‌coast of ‌the Atlantic Ocean, with significant support from the ‌RDIF (Russian Direct Investment Fund),” Novak said. Under a deal announced this month by US president Donald Trump, Russia agreed ‌to supply diesel to global markets in an effort to lower fuel ​prices in return for Trump temporarily lifting US sanctions on Russian fuel. Reuters reported that the Malta-flagged ⁠medium-sized tanker Agioi Fanendes, loaded with ultra-low sulphur diesel, is expected to arrive in ‌the US on 7 November.

The White House has said that Russia and Ukraine have agreed to a ceasefire in the Russian-occupied city of Oleshky, where a deepening humanitarian crisis has left thousands of civilians struggling to survive. In a statement on Friday, the White House said both sides had agreed to halt all military operations in the city from 27 October to allow humanitarian aid deliveries and preparations for the evacuation of civilians. Residents of the southern Ukrainian city, which has been under Russian occupation since February 2022, have described increasingly desperate conditions amid severe shortages of food, water and electricity. An estimated 2,000 people remain in the city, with some reportedly forced to survive on weeds, boiled grass, bread and meagre rations. Both Russian and Ukrainian officials said all sides were close to agreeing to a ceasefire.

The Oleshky ceasefire comes as the US is trying to organise new talks aimed at ending the war. Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on Friday negotiators from Ukraine, Russia and the US have agreed to technical-level meetings in the first half of November in Abu Dhabi. A US official later said the three ⁠countries may hold their next talks in a couple weeks in Abu Dhabi or Switzerland. Zelenskyy said he hoped a meeting of the countries’ leaders would follow.

The peace efforts follow a rift between Washington and Kyiv in recent weeks and a series of moves by Trump seen as favouring Russia, including limitations being placed on the Starlink communication system that Ukraine uses to protect against incoming attacks. Trump said on Friday that if Ukraine still faced a problem accessing the system, he would straighten it out ​and, if necessary, speak about the matter to SpaceX CEO Elon Musk.

As the UK government prepares next week for the first budget under Andy Burnham’s leadership, EU leaders have pressed the new prime minister at a summit in Brussels to contribute more to Ukraine’s defence effort. EU officials say Canada and Japan also should do more to support Ukraine.

The UN nuclear watchdog IAEA said ⁠Fiday ​that repairs to key ⁠power infrastructure near Ukraine’s Zaporizhzhia ⁠nuclear power ​plant ‌had been completed ‌under a ‌temporary ceasefire it brokered. The repairs strengthened the plant’s connection ‌to its sole remaining external power ​line, known as Ferosplavna-1, reducing the ⁠risk of another ​loss of ​off-site ​electricity at ​Europe’s largest ‌nuclear ​power ​station.
